nodes.label: The authors' title asserts that female agency serves as an 'elephant test' for feminist porn and that immersive pornography consumption impacts male explicit and implicit associations about women in society.
nodes.note: Title-level claim; the two main claims (C2, C9) are offered as its grounds.
nodes.short: Agency is elephant test; porn impacts associations

anchors.exact: Further mixed-method analyses indicate these hypotheses are broadly supported but suboptimal for addressing important questions in critical porn research.
This study initially hypothesizes female-friendly pornography improves implicit and explicit male attitudes about women in society while female-degrading pornography damages them.
In this sense, female-friendly pornography led participants to subjectively improved attitudes about women
It is likely that immersive consumption of varying types of pornography can have significant impacts upon men

nodes.flag: The claim is stated about men's attitudes generally and about implicit association, but the participants are four men, two of whom are the authors, and the source's own quantitative result (E4) says IAT scores across a viewing session 'rarely changed'. The 'broadly supported' verdict therefore rests mainly on the four participants' self-described feelings, with no non-pornography control condition to compare against. Closing the gap would require an independent sample, a control condition and reported IAT change statistics.
nodes.label: The authors claim that immersive consumption of female-friendly pornography improves, and female-degrading pornography damages, male implicit and explicit associations about women in society, and that the data broadly support this hypothesis.
nodes.short: Friendly porn improves, degrading porn damages attitudes

anchors.exact: the variable of female agency is shown to produce statistically significant semi-paradoxical results which challenge the assumptions underlying a facile categorization of pornography into female-friendly and female-degrading subtypes.
Overall, the data indicate that apparent female agency and scene authenticity seem to be the most relevant variables with regard to pornography

This seems intrinsically linked to that which theoretically renders pornography feminist in orientation, including highly authentic scenes and those depicting high levels of female agency (cf. Stoya 2014, 202).

nodes.flag: The abstract says the agency variable produced 'statistically significant' results, but the body reports no test statistic, p-value, effect size or sample-restricted numbers for the agency/authenticity analysis; the only statistics given anywhere are two correlation coefficients between subjective ratings and arousal (E3), and the referenced Figure is absent. The Results section also states the quantitative data are 'presented in brief' as benchmarks. A reader cannot check the significance claim from what is shown.
nodes.label: The authors claim that apparent female agency and scene authenticity, together with the sexual arousal they produce, are the most relevant variables governing pornography's influence on how men view women, producing 'statistically significant' semi-paradoxical results.
nodes.note: The 'statistically weak' remark in b45 refers to the female-friendly/female-degrading contrast, not to the agency variable, so the two statements are about different analyses.
nodes.short: Agency and authenticity are the operative variables

That these influence male biases about women at the level of implicit association is also likely, especially when the consumption of pornography creates high levels of sexual arousal.

anchors.exact: Similarly, at least some pornography that appears ‘female-degrading’ (say by depicting scenes of male dominance or female depersonalization [cf. Cowan and Dunn 1994]) can actually be feminist in orientation if it preserves female agency in production and enables a perception of female agency in the viewer.
This tells us that the existing social-scientific paradigms for classifying pornography are woefully inadequate and deeply problematic.

the data here indicate significant overlaps in certain themes such as female agenticity and scene authenticity that may not be readily apparent by a coarse categorization into ‘female-friendly’ and ‘female-degrading’ typologies.

nodes.flag: The study's data are viewers' impressions of on-screen agency and authenticity (M4), yet the conclusion invokes 'agency in production' and, in b58, whether a performer 'finds veridical sexual fulfillment'. Nothing in the design observes performers, production conditions or performer intent, so the source cannot distinguish genuine agency from a convincing performance of it—an alternative the authors themselves raise in b55 ('when she is faking her enthusiasm') but do not resolve.
nodes.label: The authors claim that some pornography appearing female-degrading can be feminist if it preserves female agency in production and enables perceived agency in the viewer, so the female-friendly/female-degrading paradigm for classifying pornography is inadequate.
nodes.short: Degrading porn can be feminist; paradigm inadequate

nodes.flag: The only grounds offered are the two authors' account of their own change in outlook; the claim is stated for '(male) pornography consumers' generally. No participant other than the PIs is reported to have disrupted sexism, and no measure of sexism before and after reflection is given.

nodes.flag: The stated numbers do not agree: half of 1,164 is 582, not 528 (528 is half of PI1's 1,056 tests alone). Either the total or the per-category count is wrong, and no per-participant or per-category IAT change results are reported that would let a reader tell which.

anchors.exact: PI1 saw a general decrease in all of his IAT scores as the study proceeded. This corresponded with his increased levels of arousal in viewing female-degrading scenes, which he ‘got a taste for.’

PI2, by contrast, saw a general increase in all of his IAT scores over the course of the study, and this corresponded most clearly with increased levels of sexual arousal corresponding to highly authentic scenes of any type.

Indeed, the clearest results were obtained when considering only those viewing sessions for which participants subjectively rated high levels of apparent female agency and scene authenticity (values of 4 or 5), regardless of the type of scene.

For instance, having developed ‘a taste’ for female-degrading scenes seemed to impact attitudes about women negatively while coming to enjoy authentic scenes, regardless of their content, seemed to improve these attitudes longitudinally (cf. Liberman 2015).

nodes.flag: Two individuals drifted in opposite directions over a year, and each drift is attributed to a different viewing-related cause ('taste' for degrading scenes vs. enjoyment of authentic scenes). With n=2, no control period, and a year of other life events and repeated IAT practice unaccounted for, the design cannot separate these attributions from coincidence or from post hoc explanation. The Figure the text refers to is not present.
nodes.label: Over the year, PI1's IAT scores drifted downward as he 'got a taste for' female-degrading scenes, while PI2's drifted upward with arousal at highly authentic scenes; effects were clearest when sessions were restricted to arousal or agency/authenticity ratings of 4–5.
nodes.short: PI IAT drift tracks taste and authenticity

Correlations this close to 1 are consistent with the agency and authenticity ratings simply re-expressing how aroused the viewer felt, rather than measuring a distinct property of the scene; the source does not test this alternative (for example with independent raters).

anchors.exact: we used the Harvard Project Implicit Gender-Science implicit association test (IAT) as a proxy for attitudes about women in society.
Quantitative data for this study were obtained by taking the Harvard Project Implicit Gender-Science IAT test both before and after immersively viewing pornographic videos of each experimental type.
each took the Harvard Project Implicit Gender-Science IAT test to achieve a baseline measurement

nodes.flag: A single gender–science association test stands in for 'attitudes about women in society' and, in the title, for 'explicit and implicit associations'. The source names it a proxy but then reads IAT drift as change in how men 'view women in science/society' generally; whether gender–science sorting speed captures objectification or sexism is not addressed. Repeated administration (over 1,000 times per PI) as a possible source of drift is also not discussed.
nodes.label: Attitudes were measured with the Harvard Project Implicit Gender-Science IAT, used as a proxy for attitudes about women in society, taken before and after each roughly two-hour viewing block and coded from -3 to +3.
nodes.short: Gender-Science IAT pre/post, coded -3 to +3

anchors.exact: similar data were obtained from two male volunteers trained in the experimental method and instructed on how to record and report their results. These volunteers were recruited directly by the PIs from among their peer group.
From February 6, 2017, through February 9, 2018, each of the PIs undertook the following protocol approximately five days per week
PI1 viewing roughly 1056 hours of pornographic videos

nodes.flag: The investigators are also the main subjects: 2,048 of 2,328 IAT results come from the two PIs, who knew the hypotheses, chose and filtered the stimuli, rated their own arousal and agency perceptions, interviewed each other and coded the transcripts. Volunteer data were self-recorded and self-reported. There is no blinding, no independent rater and no participant outside the authors' circle, so expectancy effects cannot be separated from findings.
nodes.label: Participants were the two male principal investigators, who ran the protocol on themselves about five days a week from February 2017 to February 2018, plus two male volunteers recruited from the PIs' peer group who self-reported 60 and 220 hours respectively.
nodes.short: Two PIs as subjects plus two peer volunteers

anchors.exact: Videos were classified into two broad experimental types, ‘female-friendly’ and ‘female-degrading,’ by applying two filters, one gross and one fine.
The gross filter selected pornographic videos from online ‘tube’ sites

A finer filter was then applied to videos by a real-time subjective assessment of the content: If a video was insufficiently female-friendly or female-degrading in the subjective determina-tion of the viewer, that scene would be terminated, and the viewer would progress to a new video within the experimental category.

nodes.flag: The category a scene ended up in depended on the same viewer's in-the-moment judgment that is later analysed as an outcome (perceived agency, arousal). Scenes that felt insufficiently 'degrading' were dropped, so the female-degrading sample is pre-selected toward scenes the viewer found convincingly degrading—and, given E3, possibly arousing. The source also notes in b20 that tube-site tags are largely a marketing tool, yet uses them as the gross filter without reporting how many scenes each filter discarded.
nodes.label: Heterosexual videos were assigned to 'female-friendly' or 'female-degrading' first by tube-site tags and then by a real-time subjective judgment of the viewer, who abandoned any scene he felt did not sufficiently fit its category.
nodes.short: Tag-based then subjective category filtering

anchors.exact: subjective levels of arousal, including compulsive impulses to masturbate, were recorded and coded on a scale from zero to five

Third, subjects were encouraged to note their subjective assessments of portrayals of apparent female agency and scene authenticity (desire to be involved in the scene and apparent chemistry between/among performers).
subjects met with the PIs, who also met with each other, once per week during experimental periods for semi-structured interviews/discussions
This led to the incorporation of agency and authenticity as pertinent subjective variables after four weeks.

nodes.label: Qualitative data comprised participants' notes on attitudes, self-rated arousal (0–5), self-rated apparent female agency and scene authenticity (0–5, added after four weeks), and weekly semi-structured interviews transcribed and coded thematically with a grounded-theory approach.
nodes.note: 'Authenticity' is operationalised partly as the viewer's own 'desire to be involved in the scene', which overlaps by definition with arousal. Agency/authenticity ratings do not exist for the first four weeks of viewing.
nodes.short: Self-ratings and interviews, thematically coded
